contents.html: Category N2 is for submissions of threshold schemes for primitives of NIST-specified public-key encryption (PKE) schemes (see submission requirements in Section 10.2). In practice, PKE is often used as a building block in other standardized schemes, which in turn are used to enable pair-wise key-establishment (2KE) protocols. Future schemes may be added to this scope, once NIST-standardized.
contents.html_ja: カテゴリ N2 は、NIST が規定する公開鍵暗号化（PKE）方式のプリミティブに対するしきい値方式の提出のためのものです（提出要件は第 10.2 節を参照）。実際には、PKE は、他の標準化された方式の構成要素としてよく使われ、それらが 2 者間の鍵確立（2KE）プロトコルを可能にするために使われます。将来の方式は、NIST が標準化した時点で、この範囲に追加される場合があります。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p88（scale 1.4）の画像と照合し一致

contents.html: NIST standards with PKE schemes. NIST specifies PKE schemes in the standards for (i) RSA-based 2KE [SP800-56B-Rev2], and (ii) the Module-Lattice-based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism (ML-KEM) [FIPS-203]. These standards use PKE encryption (Enc) and decryption (Dec) primitives as building blocks to construct higher-level schemes, namely key-agreement schemes (KAS), key-transport schemes (KTS), and KEMs (see Appendices A.2.1 and A.2.2). In turn, all of these can be used to enable particular instantiations of 2KE, to allow two parties to agree on a secret key, without an eavesdropper learning it. In these applications, the core use of the PKE scheme is in allowing one party to encrypt a random contribution (i.e., a seed that will affect the derivation of an agreed key) and send it securely (i.e., with confidentiality) to a decryptor party.
contents.html_ja: PKE 方式を含む NIST 標準。 NIST は、(i) RSA ベースの 2KE [SP800-56B-Rev2] と (ii) モジュール格子ベースの鍵カプセル化メカニズム（ML-KEM）[FIPS-203] の標準で PKE 方式を規定しています。これらの標準は、PKE の暗号化（Enc）と復号（Dec）のプリミティブを構成要素として、より上位レベルの方式、すなわち鍵合意方式（KAS）、鍵輸送方式（KTS）、KEM を構築しています（附属書 A.2.1 と A.2.2 を参照）。さらに、これらのすべてを使って、2KE の特定のインスタンス化を可能にし、盗聴者に知られることなく 2 者が共通鍵に合意できるようにします。これらの応用での PKE 方式の中心的な用途は、一方の当事者がランダムな寄与（すなわち、合意される鍵の導出に影響するシード）を暗号化し、復号側の当事者に安全に（すなわち機密性を保って）送れるようにすることです。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p88（scale 1.4）の画像と照合し一致。行末のソフトハイフンで分かれた語（decryption、Appendices）を連結

contents.html: In typical 2KE application, based on a KAS, KTS, or KEM, it is important avoid misuse of the low-level PKE primitives, which poses a security risk (e.g., a dangerous decryption oracle). Any actual proposal of a threshold scheme for replacing a party in a full-fledged PKE-based 2KE application needs to consider the security of the entire system.
contents.html_ja: KAS、KTS、KEM に基づく典型的な 2KE の応用では、低レベルの PKE プリミティブの誤用を避けることが重要です。誤用はセキュリティ上のリスク（危険な復号オラクルなど）をもたらします。本格的な PKE ベースの 2KE の応用で当事者を置き換えるためのしきい値方式を実際に提案する場合は、システム全体のセキュリティを考慮する必要があります。

contents.html: Primitives of interest. Enc outputs a ciphertext \(C = \mathrm{Enc}(pubKey, M[, R])\), as an encryption of an input plaintext message \(M\), using a public encryption key \(pubKey\), and optionally (i.e., depending on the scheme) a random value \(R\) that directly enables probabilistic encryption. Correspondingly, Dec outputs the original plaintext \(M = \mathrm{Dec}(privKey, C)\), as decryption of an input ciphertext, using the private decryption key \(privKey\).
contents.html_ja: 関心のあるプリミティブ。 Enc は、入力の平文メッセージ \(M\) の暗号化として、公開暗号化鍵 \(pubKey\) と、任意で（すなわち方式に応じて）確率的暗号化を直接可能にするランダム値 \(R\) を使って、暗号文 \(C = \mathrm{Enc}(pubKey, M[, R])\) を出力します。これに対応して、Dec は、入力の暗号文の復号として、秘密の復号鍵 \(privKey\) を使って、元の平文 \(M = \mathrm{Dec}(privKey, C)\) を出力します。

contents.html: RSA Encryption Primitive (RSAEP): Obtains a ciphertext \(c = \mathrm{RSAEP}(e, m) = m^e \bmod N\), using the public key \(e\) to encrypt the plaintext \(m\). RSAEP is assumed to be a one-way function. Being deterministic, it does not provide on its own the IND-CPA property of an encryption scheme. Providing semantic security and beyond requires a higher-level construction (see §A.2.1.2), including randomness.
contents.html_ja: RSA 暗号化プリミティブ（RSAEP）: 公開鍵 \(e\) を用いて平文 \(m\) を暗号化し、暗号文 \(c = \mathrm{RSAEP}(e, m) = m^e \bmod N\) を得ます。RSAEP は一方向関数であると仮定されています。決定的であるため、それ自体では暗号方式の IND-CPA 性を提供しません。意味的安全性やそれ以上を提供するには、ランダム性を含む上位レベルの構成（§A.2.1.2 を参照）が必要です。

contents.html: RSA Decryption Primitive (RSADP): Recovers the plaintext \(m = c^d \mathrm{mod} \mathrm{N}\), by calculating \(m = \mathrm{RSADP}(privKey, c)\), where the private key privKey is used to decrypt the ciphertext \(c\). The input privKey is acceptable in three possible formats [SP800-56B-Rev2, §6.2.2]: basic \((N, d)\), prime-factor \((p, q, d)\), and Chinese-remainder theorem (CRT) \((N, e, d, p, q, dP, dQ, qInv)\), where [SP800-56B-Rev2, §3.2] \((p, q)\) is the pair of secret prime factors of \(N\), \(dP\) is \(d \bmod (p-1)\), \(dQ\) is \(d \bmod (q-1)\), and \(qInv\) is the inverse of \(q \bmod p\).
contents.html_ja: RSA 復号プリミティブ（RSADP）: \(m = \mathrm{RSADP}(privKey, c)\) を計算することで平文 \(m = c^d \mathrm{mod} \mathrm{N}\) を復元します。ここで、秘密鍵 privKey を使って暗号文 \(c\) を復号します。入力 privKey は、3 つの形式 [SP800-56B-Rev2, §6.2.2] で受け付けられます。基本形式 \((N, d)\)、素因数形式 \((p, q, d)\)、中国剰余定理（CRT）形式 \((N, e, d, p, q, dP, dQ, qInv)\) です。ここで [SP800-56B-Rev2, §3.2]、\((p, q)\) は \(N\) の秘密の素因数のペア、\(dP\) は \(d \bmod (p-1)\)、\(dQ\) は \(d \bmod (q-1)\)、\(qInv\) は \(q \bmod p\) の逆元です。

contents.html: FIPS-203 is the first NIST standard to specify a PQ-PKE scheme (dubbed K-PKE), whose use is only approved to support ML-KEM. The present subcategory (N2.2) is interested in the core K-PKE encryption/decryption primitives: K-PKE.Encrypt (Enc) and K-PKE.Decrypt (Dec). The three approved parameter sets ML-KEM-{512,768,1024} determine corresponding parameters for K-PKE, which correspond to PQC security categories \(\theta = \{1, 3, 5\}\), if their internal RBG has security strength \(\kappa = \{128, 192, 256\}\).
contents.html_ja: FIPS-203 は、PQ-PKE 方式（K-PKE と呼ばれる）を規定した NIST 初の標準で、その使用は ML-KEM の支援のためにのみ承認されています。このサブカテゴリ（N2.2）は、中核となる K-PKE の暗号化・復号プリミティブ、K-PKE.Encrypt（Enc）と K-PKE.Decrypt（Dec）に関心があります。承認された 3 つのパラメータセット ML-KEM-{512,768,1024} が K-PKE の対応するパラメータを決定し、内部の RBG のセキュリティ強度が \(\kappa = \{128, 192, 256\}\) であれば、PQC セキュリティカテゴリ \(\theta = \{1, 3, 5\}\) に対応します。

contents.html: For simplicity, the following text omits the prefix K-PKE, and abbreviates the primitives’ names. For the purposes of this subcategory (N2.2), it is useful to conceptualize Enc’ as a probabilistic variant of Enc, as follows: Enc’ has the same input/output syntax, but randomly selects the internal values \((y[i], e_1[i], e_2)\), instead of computing them pseudorandomly from the input seed \(r\). Effectively, Enc’ ignores the input seed \(r\). For threshold purposes (see §10.6), a key observation is that Enc’ and Enc are interchangeable with regard to Dec. In particular, Dec(Enc’(...)) = Dec(Enc(...)) for any \(\mathrm{ek}_{\mathrm{PKE}}\), \(m\), and \(r\).
contents.html_ja: 簡単のため、以下の文章では K-PKE という接頭辞を省略し、プリミティブの名前を略記します。このサブカテゴリ（N2.2）の目的上、Enc’ を Enc の確率的な変種として、次のように捉えると有用です。Enc’ は Enc と同じ入出力構文を持ちますが、内部値 \((y[i], e_1[i], e_2)\) を、入力シード \(r\) から擬似ランダムに計算する代わりに、ランダムに選択します。実質的に、Enc’ は入力シード \(r\) を無視します。しきい値の目的（§10.6 を参照）では、Enc’ と Enc が Dec に関して互換性があることが重要な観察です。特に、任意の \(\mathrm{ek}_{\mathrm{PKE}}\)、\(m\)、\(r\) について、Dec(Enc’(...)) = Dec(Enc(...)) です。

contents.html: Conventional ML-KEM. Ignoring KeyGen, the ML-KEM specifies Encaps and Decaps algorithms, each of which relies on an auxiliary internal function (named with a suffix “_internal”), which in turn is based on primitives from the K-PKE scheme. Table 14 lists these relationships. Essentially, the ML-KEM.{Encaps, Decaps} primitives are based on K-PKE.{Enc, Dec} and a number of pseudorandom calculations. They are meant to ensure useful security properties (e.g., IND-CCA) and functionality (e.g., suitability for 2KE). The transformation is efficient in the conventional (i.e., non-threshold) setting, where the computation of NIST-standardized PRFs on secret material is cheap.
contents.html_ja: 従来型の ML-KEM。 KeyGen を除くと、ML-KEM は Encaps と Decaps のアルゴリズムを規定しており、それぞれが補助的な内部関数（接尾辞「_internal」を付けた名前）に依拠し、それがさらに K-PKE 方式のプリミティブに基づいています。表 14 に、これらの関係を示します。本質的に、ML-KEM.{Encaps, Decaps} プリミティブは K-PKE.{Enc, Dec} といくつかの擬似ランダムな計算に基づいています。これらは、有用なセキュリティ特性（IND-CCA など）と機能（2KE への適合性など）を確保することを意図しています。この変換は、従来型（すなわちしきい値なし）の設定では、NIST が標準化した PRF を秘密素材に対して計算するコストが小さいため、効率的です。

contents.html: Threshold ML-KEM: Going from threshold K-PKE.{Enc, Dec} to threshold ML-KEM.{Encaps, Decaps} is impractically expensive in the threshold setting, due to requiring distributed computation of threshold-unfriendly PRFs. Teams can still explore the complexity of such implementations, and possibly propose threshold-friendlier alternatives, e.g., based on threshold-friendlier symmetric primitives (see category S3 in Section 11.3), or threshold-friendlier PKE-based KEM schemes (see category S2 in Section 11.2).

contents.html: Threshold AES enciphering/deciphering. In the threshold AES case of interest, the key-holder party is distributed into multiple parties (i.e., a secret sharing of the key is distributed across the parties), who then compute the ciphertext without reconstructing the key. If implemented in an SSIO-threshold manner, then no party within the decentralized key-holder learns the plaintext or ciphertext.

contents.html: Comparison with oblivious AES evaluation. Threshold AES enciphering with SSI-plaintext and SSO-ciphertext is similar to but different from two-party oblivious AES evaluation, which is a common secure 2-party computation (S2PC) benchmark in the MPC literature. In the latter, one party (the receiver) knows the plaintext and another party (the key-holder) knows the key. They both keep their inputs private, yet enable the receiver to learn the corresponding ciphertext. Despite the differences, the building blocks presented for resolving threshold AES may also be useful for implementing oblivious AES evaluation.
contents.html_ja: オブリビアス AES 評価との比較。 SSI 平文と SSO 暗号文によるしきい値 AES 暗号化は、MPC の文献で一般的な安全な 2 者間計算（S2PC）のベンチマークである 2 者間のオブリビアス AES 評価と、似ていますが異なります。後者では、一方の当事者（受信者）が平文を知り、もう一方の当事者（鍵保持者）が鍵を知っています。両者は入力を秘密にしたまま、受信者が対応する暗号文を知ることを可能にします。相違点はあるものの、しきい値 AES を解決するために提示された構成要素は、オブリビアス AES 評価の実装にも有用な場合があります。

contents.html: Conventional KeyGen. A KeyGen determines a secret key (sometimes called a private key) that is needed by subsequent primitives. Depending on the crypto-system, the KeyGen may also generate a related public key. For example, the KeyGen primitive of a digital signature scheme produces a private/public key-pair. The private key is used to sign messages, and the public key is used to verify signatures. A typical security requirement for the secret key is high entropy, which is obtained in case of uniformity in the corresponding key space.
contents.html_ja: 従来型の KeyGen。KeyGen は、後続のプリミティブが必要とする秘密の鍵（secret key。private key、すなわち秘密鍵と呼ばれる場合もあります）を決定します。暗号システムによっては、KeyGen が関連する公開鍵も生成する場合があります。たとえば、デジタル署名方式の KeyGen プリミティブは、署名用秘密鍵と公開鍵のペアを生成します。署名用秘密鍵はメッセージへの署名に使われ、公開鍵は署名の検証に使われます。この秘密の鍵に対する典型的なセキュリティ要件は高いエントロピーであり、これは対応する鍵空間で一様である場合に得られます。

contents.html: “Scalar multiplication” versus “exponentiation”. Group operations over elliptic curves are usually described with additive notation. When a public key \(Q\) is determined by a repeated sum of the base-point \(G\), a secret number \(d\) of times, their relationship is mathematically expressed as a scalar multiplication (i.e., \(Q = d \cdot G\)). However, the literature often refers to this as an “exponentiation”, and correspondingly identifies the secret key as the “discrete log” of the public key. This a tolerated misnomer due to the prior popularization of schemes described with multiplicative notation (e.g., \(q = g^d\)).

contents.html: The size of an RSA modulus determines an upper bound on the security strength of the RSA-related primitive (i.e., signing, encryption or decryption). The following specific cases are fixed: \(|N| = 3072\) for \(\kappa \approx 128\), \(|N| = 7680\) for \(\kappa \approx 192\), and \(|N| = 15360\) for \(\kappa \approx 256\). By standard, the RSA modulus length \(|N|\) must be a multiple of 8. For benchmarking purposes, this Threshold Call further suggests that it be a multiple of 512. Implementations that aim for \(\kappa \notin \{128, 192, 256\}\) can interpolate an RSA modulus size by rounding up to a multiple of 512 the solution (for \(|N|\)) of \(\kappa \ln(2) = \sqrt[3]{(64/9) \cdot (|N| \ln(2)) \cdot \ln^2(|N| \ln(2))} - 4.69\), from “§7.5 Strength of Key Establishment Methods” of the “FIPS 140-2 Implementation Guidance” [IG-FIPS-140-2]. For example, \(\kappa \approx 224\) the result is \(|N| = 10{,}752\).
contents.html_ja: RSA モジュラスのサイズは、RSA 関連プリミティブ（すなわち署名、暗号化または復号）のセキュリティ強度の上限を決定します。次の具体的な場合が固定されています。\(\kappa \approx 128\) では \(|N| = 3072\)、\(\kappa \approx 192\) では \(|N| = 7680\)、\(\kappa \approx 256\) では \(|N| = 15360\) です。標準では、RSA モジュラスの長さ \(|N|\) は 8 の倍数でなければなりません。ベンチマークの目的で、このしきい値公募は、さらに 512 の倍数とすることを提案します。\(\kappa \notin \{128, 192, 256\}\) を目指す実装では、「FIPS 140-2 Implementation Guidance」[IG-FIPS-140-2] の「§7.5 Strength of Key Establishment Methods」にある \(\kappa \ln(2) = \sqrt[3]{(64/9) \cdot (|N| \ln(2)) \cdot \ln^2(|N| \ln(2))} - 4.69\) の解（\(|N|\) について）を 512 の倍数に切り上げることで、RSA モジュラスのサイズを補間できます。たとえば、\(\kappa \approx 224\) では、結果は \(|N| = 10{,}752\) です。

contents.html: K-PKE.KeyGen. See Algorithm 13 in FIPS-203. Given a 32-byte input seed \(d\), the algorithm starts by pseudorandomly generating a public seed \(\rho\) and a private seed \(\sigma\). The public seed \(\rho\) is used to generate a matrix \(\hat{\mathbf{A}}\). The private seed \(\sigma\) is used to generate a secret vector \(\hat{\mathbf{s}}\) and a secret noise \(\hat{\mathbf{e}}\). The pseudorandom samplings are based on the algorithm “SamplePolyCBD”, and the hat \(\hat{\ }\) signifies an application of the Number Theoretic Transform (NTT). The other component of the public key is then obtained by the linear combination \(\hat{\mathbf{t}} = \hat{\mathbf{A}} \circ \hat{\mathbf{s}} + \hat{\mathbf{e}}\). The output encryption key is \((\hat{\mathbf{t}}, \rho)\) (where \(\rho\) is the seed of \(\hat{\mathbf{A}}\)). The output private key is \(\hat{\mathbf{s}}\) (i.e., could be derived from \(\sigma\)).
contents.html_ja: K-PKE.KeyGen。 FIPS-203 のアルゴリズム 13 を参照してください。32 バイトの入力シード \(d\) が与えられると、アルゴリズムはまず、公開シード \(\rho\) と秘密シード \(\sigma\) を擬似ランダムに生成します。公開シード \(\rho\) は行列 \(\hat{\mathbf{A}}\) の生成に使われます。秘密シード \(\sigma\) は、秘密ベクトル \(\hat{\mathbf{s}}\) と秘密のノイズ \(\hat{\mathbf{e}}\) の生成に使われます。擬似ランダムなサンプリングはアルゴリズム「SamplePolyCBD」に基づき、ハット \(\hat{\ }\) は数論変換（NTT）の適用を表します。公開鍵のもう 1 つの構成要素は、線形結合 \(\hat{\mathbf{t}} = \hat{\mathbf{A}} \circ \hat{\mathbf{s}} + \hat{\mathbf{e}}\) によって得られます。出力される暗号化鍵は \((\hat{\mathbf{t}}, \rho)\)（\(\rho\) は \(\hat{\mathbf{A}}\) のシード）です。出力される秘密鍵は \(\hat{\mathbf{s}}\)（すなわち、\(\sigma\) から導出できる）です。

contents.html: ML-DSA.KeyGen. See Algorithms 6 and 1 in FIPS-204. ML-DSA.KeyGen selects a random 32-byte seed \(\xi\) and calls ML-DSA.KeyGen_internal with that seed as input. The latter is then deterministic, using various pseudorandom sampling routines, starting with generating a public seed \(\rho\), a private seed \(\rho\)’, and another private seed \(K\). The public seed \(\rho\) is used to generate a matrix \(\hat{\mathbf{A}}\). The private seed \(\rho\)’ is used to generate secret vectors \(\mathbf{s_1}\) and \(\mathbf{s_2}\), and then compute the linear combination \(\mathbf{t} = \mathrm{NTT}^{-1}(\hat{\mathbf{A}} \circ \mathrm{NTT}(\mathbf{s_1})) + \mathbf{s_2}\), which can be parsed into \((\mathbf{t_1}, \mathbf{t_0})\) using the routine “’Power2Round”. Finally, the public verification key is \((\rho, \mathbf{t_1})\), and the signing key is composed of \((K, \mathbf{s_1}, \mathbf{s_2}, \mathbf{t_0})\), and (an encoding of) the public components \(\rho\) and \(\mathbf{t_1}\), and what can be derived from them (e.g., \(tr\)).
contents.html_ja: ML-DSA.KeyGen。FIPS-204 のアルゴリズム 6 と 1 を参照してください。ML-DSA.KeyGen はランダムな 32 バイトのシード \(\xi\) を選択し、そのシードを入力として ML-DSA.KeyGen_internal を呼び出します。後者はその後、さまざまな擬似ランダムサンプリングルーチンを使って決定的に動作し、まず公開シード \(\rho\)、秘密シード \(\rho\)’、もう 1 つの秘密シード \(K\) を生成します。公開シード \(\rho\) は行列 \(\hat{\mathbf{A}}\) の生成に使われます。秘密シード \(\rho\)’ は秘密ベクトル \(\mathbf{s_1}\) と \(\mathbf{s_2}\) の生成に使われ、次に線形結合 \(\mathbf{t} = \mathrm{NTT}^{-1}(\hat{\mathbf{A}} \circ \mathrm{NTT}(\mathbf{s_1})) + \mathbf{s_2}\) を計算します。この結果は、ルーチン「’Power2Round」を使って \((\mathbf{t_1}, \mathbf{t_0})\) に分解できます。最後に、公開検証鍵は \((\rho, \mathbf{t_1})\) であり、署名鍵は \((K, \mathbf{s_1}, \mathbf{s_2}, \mathbf{t_0})\)、公開構成要素 \(\rho\) と \(\mathbf{t_1}\) の符号化、およびそれらから導出できるもの（例: \(tr\)）で構成されます。

contents.html: Conventional generation. Various primitives require a randomly generated secret bit-string or secret integer within an interval, without the need for a corresponding public component. For example, this is the case for an AES key, a secret-key for encapsulation under an RSA PKE, a nonce for use in other schemes, and a salt for a KDM or KC in the scope of a 2KA. Usually, these KeyGens are required to follow NIST-approved RBG methods [SP800-90A-R1; SP800-90B; SP800-90C], to obtain either pseudorandomness or true randomness.
contents.html_ja: 従来型の生成。さまざまなプリミティブでは、対応する公開構成要素を必要とせずに、ランダムに生成された秘密のビット列または区間内の秘密の整数が必要です。たとえば、AES 鍵、RSA PKE によるカプセル化に用いる共通鍵、他の方式で用いるナンス、および 2KA の範囲内の KDM または KC 用のソルトがこれに当たります。通常、これらの KeyGen は、擬似ランダム性または真のランダム性のいずれかを得るため、NIST が承認した RBG 方式 [SP800-90A-R1; SP800-90B; SP800-90C] に従う必要があります。

contents.html: Category S5 (see submission requirements in Section 11.5) allows for the submission of FHE schemes. Informally speaking, an FHE scheme allows for arbitrary computations over encrypted data. Being an encryption scheme, in includes KeyGen, encryption (Enc) and decryption (Dec) algorithms Being fully homomorphic it also includes algorithms for the efficient homomorphic evaluation, over the ciphertext space (\(\mathcal{C}\)), of a “complete basis” of operations from the plaintext space (\(\mathcal{P}\)) (e.g., see Ref. [HES, §1.1.1]). The composition of these operations allows for arbitrary computations.
contents.html_ja: カテゴリ S5（提出要件は第 11.5 節を参照）では、FHE 方式を提出できます。大まかに言えば、FHE 方式は暗号化されたデータに対する任意の計算を可能にします。暗号方式であるため、KeyGen、暗号化（Enc）、復号（Dec）のアルゴリズムを含みます。完全準同型であるため、平文空間（\(\mathcal{P}\)）の演算の「完全基底」（例: 文献 [HES, §1.1.1] を参照）を暗号文空間（\(\mathcal{C}\)）上で効率的に準同型評価するアルゴリズムも含みます。これらの演算を合成することで、任意の計算が可能になります。

contents.html: In an “oblivious” PRF evaluation there is a client (\(A\)) holding a secret plaintext \(m\), and a server (\(S\)) holding a secret key \(k\). They interact in a way that allows the client to privately learn the output of the PRF evaluation over the plaintext, while both parties remain oblivious to the other party’s input. By replacing the PRF with the AES blockcipher (a PRP), the client learns the AES-enciphering of the plaintext \(m\). Oblivious AES-enciphering is a typical benchmark case for secure 2-party computation, typically using techniques such as garbled circuits and/or oblivious transfer. Compared with an FHE-based solution, usual S2PC protocols lead to faster execution, but also larger communication complexity.
contents.html_ja: 「オブリビアス」PRF 評価では、秘密の平文 \(m\) を持つクライアント（\(A\)）と、秘密鍵 \(k\) を持つサーバー（\(S\)）がいます。両者は、クライアントがその平文に対する PRF 評価の出力を秘密裏に得られ、両当事者が互いの入力を知らないままでいられるようにやり取りします。PRF を AES ブロック暗号（PRP）に置き換えると、クライアントは平文 \(m\) の AES 暗号化結果を得ます。オブリビアス AES 暗号化は、安全な 2 者間計算の典型的なベンチマークケースであり、通常、ガーブル回路またはオブリビアス転送などの技術が使われます。FHE ベースの解決策と比べると、通常の S2PC プロトコルは実行が速い一方、通信量は大きくなります。

contents.html: FHE-Decrypt. The client \(B\) FHE-decrypts the received ciphertext \(H\), to obtain the AES enciphering of the secret plaintext: \(\mathrm{AES.Enc}_k(m) = \mathrm{FHE.Dec}_d(H)\).
contents.html_ja: FHE 復号。 クライアント \(B\) が受信した暗号文 \(H\) を FHE 復号し、秘密の平文の AES 暗号化 \(\mathrm{AES.Enc}_k(m) = \mathrm{FHE.Dec}_d(H)\) を得ます。

contents.html: 4a. (Optional) Prove correctness. The server \(S\) may also send to client \(B\) a ZKPoK string \(\pi = \mathrm{ZKPoK.Prove}[k; (H, C) : \mathrm{FHE.Hom}[\mathrm{AES.Enc}_k](C) = H]\), thus ZK-proving knowledge of a secret AES key (\(k\)) that is consistent with the homomorphic operation that transformed the initial FHE ciphertext \(C\) into the final FHE ciphertext \(H\). A more sophisticated ZKPoK can also be used to prove consistency with some additional public commitment of the AES key \(k\).
contents.html_ja: 4a. （任意）正しさの証明。 サーバー \(S\) は、ZKPoK 文字列 \(\pi = \mathrm{ZKPoK.Prove}[k; (H, C) : \mathrm{FHE.Hom}[\mathrm{AES.Enc}_k](C) = H]\) もクライアント \(B\) に送ることができ、これにより、最初の FHE 暗号文 \(C\) を最終的な FHE 暗号文 \(H\) に変換した準同型操作と整合する AES の共通鍵（\(k\)）の知識をゼロ知識で証明します。より高度な ZKPoK を使って、AES 鍵 \(k\) の追加の公開コミットメントとの整合性を証明することもできます。

contents.html: 4b. Verify the proof. Anyone with the FHE ciphertexts (\(C\), \(H\)) can verify the correctness of the ZKPoK \(\pi\), by checking \(\mathtt{true} \overset{?}{=} \mathrm{ZKPoK.Verify}(\pi, (H, C), \mathrm{AES.Enc})\).
contents.html_ja: 4b. 証明の検証。 FHE 暗号文（\(C\)、\(H\)）を持つ誰もが、\(\mathtt{true} \overset{?}{=} \mathrm{ZKPoK.Verify}(\pi, (H, C), \mathrm{AES.Enc})\) を検査することで、ZKPoK \(\pi\) の正しさを検証できます。

contents.html: In usual ZKP terminology [ZkpComRef], a ZKPoK is used to prove a statement of knowledge, such as knowledge of a secret witness (\(w\)) that satisfies a given relation (\(R\)) with a public instance (\(x\)) such that \(R(x, w)\) is true. For example, a ZKPoK of a private RSA key can have as instance the public RSA modulus \(N\), as secret witness the pair (\(p, q\)) of prime factors, and as relation the predicate that returns true if and only if the input instance \(N\) is a valid product of two secret primes. Additional refinements can be considered (e.g., proving the two primes have the same bit-length, and are both 3 mod 4).
contents.html_ja: 通常の ZKP の用語 [ZkpComRef] では、ZKPoK は知識の言明を証明するために使われます。たとえば、公開インスタンス（\(x\)）との関係（\(R\)）を満たす秘密の証人（\(w\)）の知識であり、\(R(x, w)\) が真となるものです。たとえば、RSA 秘密鍵の ZKPoK では、公開 RSA 法 \(N\) をインスタンス、素因数のペア（\(p, q\)）を秘密の証人、入力インスタンス \(N\) が 2 つの秘密の素数の有効な積である場合に限り true を返す述語を関係とすることができます。追加の精緻化も考えられます（たとえば、2 つの素数が同じビット長であり、どちらも 3 mod 4 であることの証明）。

contents.html: From a ZKPoK to a signature. Since a non-interactive ZKPoK (NIZKPoK) allows for binding data (e.g., a message) to a proof, there is a tight relationship to signatures. For example, an EdDSA/Schnorr signature (see Appendix A.1.1) is a message-bound (transferable) NIZKPoK of the discrete log of the public key. Also, a ZKPoK of an AES key that connects a plaintext to a ciphertext can be the basis of a signature scheme, e.g., as observed in some schemes submitted to the NIST-PQC process [Proj-PQC].
contents.html_ja: ZKPoK から署名へ。 非対話型 ZKPoK（NIZKPoK）はデータ（メッセージなど）を証明に結び付けられるため、署名と密接な関係があります。たとえば、EdDSA/Schnorr 署名（附属書 A.1.1 を参照）は、公開鍵の離散対数についてのメッセージに結び付けられた（転送可能な）NIZKPoK です。また、平文と暗号文を結び付ける AES 鍵の ZKPoK は、署名方式の基礎となりえます。たとえば、NIST-PQC プロセス [Proj-PQC] に提出された一部の方式で見られるとおりです。

contents.html: ZKP of knowledge (versus of correctness). The proofs in scope are ZKPoKs, but can also serve the purpose of ZK-proving the correctness of the secret data (whose knowledge is being proven) and of the corresponding public data (e.g., that they are consistently related and satisfy some claimed property). In the literature, a ZKP of correctness is sometimes also known as a ZKP of “language membership”.
contents.html_ja: 知識の ZKP（正しさの ZKP と対比）。 対象となる証明は ZKPoK ですが、（知識が証明される）秘密データと、対応する公開データの正しさ（たとえば、それらが整合的に関連し、主張される性質を満たすこと）をゼロ知識で証明する目的にも使えます。文献では、正しさの ZKP は「言語所属」の ZKP とも呼ばれることがあります。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p103（scale 1.4）の画像と照合し一致

contents.html: Interactiveness. A ZKPoK can involve interaction between the prover and verifier, or be non-interactive (i.e., a NIZKPoK consisting of a single message/transcript that is sent from the prover to the verifier). If it is succinct, then it is called a zk-SNARK (succinct non-interactive ZK-argument of knowledge).
contents.html_ja: 対話性。 ZKPoK は、証明者と検証者の間のやり取りを伴う場合も、非対話型（すなわち、証明者から検証者に送られる単一のメッセージ・トランスクリプトから成る NIZKPoK）の場合もあります。簡潔であれば、zk-SNARK（簡潔な非対話型ゼロ知識の知識論証）と呼ばれます。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p103（scale 1.4）の画像と照合し一致

contents.html: Transferability versus deniability. With a deniable (i.e., non-transferable) ZKPoK, a verifier convinced by the proof cannot transfer said confidence to a third party. This often stems from interactivity, and/or relies on local setup assumptions, such as a local common reference string or local random oracle. Other proofs, usually non-interactive, can be transferred and are publicly verifiable. Another option is a “designated-verifier” proof, which can be achieved by proving a disjunctive (“or”) statement such as “this statement is true, or I know the verifier’s private key”.
contents.html_ja: 転送可能性と否認可能性。 否認可能な（すなわち転送不可能な）ZKPoK では、証明によって納得した検証者は、その確信を第三者に転送できません。これは対話性に由来することが多く、ローカルな共通参照文字列やローカルなランダムオラクルのような、ローカルなセットアップの仮定に依拠する場合があります。それ以外の、通常は非対話型の証明は、転送可能で公開検証可能です。別の選択肢として「指定検証者」証明があり、「この言明は真である、または私は検証者の秘密鍵を知っている」のような選言（「または」）の言明を証明することで実現できます。

contents.html: Threshold ZKPoK generation (distributed prover). When the witness is secret-shared, a threshold ZKPoK protocol can generate a proof of distributed knowledge. For example, the set of parties that interacted in a DKG can distributively generate a ZKPoK (e.g., via MPC) of the corresponding secret/private key. The proof may relate to public commitments of the corresponding secret shares or/and to a corresponding public key. This ZKPoK generation can be embedded in the DKG protocol or performed afterward.
contents.html_ja: しきい値 ZKPoK の生成（分散された証明者）。証人が秘密分散されている場合、しきい値 ZKPoK プロトコルは分散された知識の証明を生成できます。たとえば、DKG でやり取りした当事者の集合は、対応する共通鍵または秘密鍵の ZKPoK を（MPC などにより）分散して生成できます。この証明は、対応する秘密シェアの公開コミットメント、および／または対応する公開鍵に関連づけられる場合があります。この ZKPoK の生成は、DKG プロトコルに組み込むことも、その後に実行することもできます。

contents.html: Threshold ZKPoK verification (distributed verifier). In a threshold ZKPoK verification, a distributed verifier interacts to verify a ZKPoK, without anyone learning the proof. This can make sense for some applications, such as when the ZKP itself or/and the instance is supposed to be private, or when a more efficient proof is possible in that setting and the ZK assurance requires non-collusion by a threshold number of verifier parties.
contents.html_ja: しきい値 ZKPoK の検証（分散された検証者）。しきい値 ZKPoK の検証では、分散された検証者がやり取りして ZKPoK を検証し、誰も証明の内容を知ることはありません。これは、ZKP 自体やインスタンスが非公開であることが想定される場合や、その設定でより効率的な証明が可能で、ZK の保証がしきい値数の検証者当事者による非共謀を必要とする場合など、一部の応用では意味を持ちえます。

contents.html: Conventional ZKPoK about distributed data. ZKPoK generation can be conventional (i.e., non-threshold) or distributed. For example, a dealer (single-party) of a secret sharing can produce a ZKPoK that enables each of the various parties of a threshold entity (i.e., the recipients of secret shares) to non-interactively verify that a given public key and a list of commitments of secret shares are consistent with an adequate secret sharing.
contents.html_ja: 分散データに関する従来型の ZKPoK。 ZKPoK の生成は、従来型（すなわちしきい値なし）でも、分散型でもかまいません。たとえば、秘密分散のディーラー（単一当事者）は、しきい値エンティティの各当事者（すなわち秘密シェアの受信者）が、与えられた公開鍵と秘密シェアのコミットメントの一覧が適切な秘密分散と整合していることを、非対話で検証できるようにする ZKPoK を生成できます。

contents.html: Revealing/hiding of threshold setting. A ZKPoK related to a public instance produced by a threshold protocol (e.g., a signature, or an RSA modulus) or to a secret-shared private witness may intentionally reveal or hide the distributed/threshold setting. For example, the threshold setting can be revealed if the proof relates to commitments of the secret shares and/or to public keys of the various parties. This can be achieved based on (i) publicly verifiable secret sharing (PVSS), or (ii) publicly-verifiable MPC. Conversely, the proof can be intentionally indistinguishable from a proof that in a conventional setting. This category for ZKPoK submissions is open to both options (i.e., revealing and hiding the existence of a secret-sharing setting).
contents.html_ja: しきい値設定の開示・秘匿。しきい値プロトコルが生成した公開インスタンス（署名や RSA 法など）、または秘密分散された秘密の証人に関連する ZKPoK は、分散・しきい値設定を意図的に開示することも、秘匿することもできます。たとえば、証明が秘密シェアのコミットメントまたは／および各当事者の公開鍵に関連する場合、しきい値設定は開示されることがあります。これは、(i) 公開検証可能な秘密分散（PVSS）、または (ii) 公開検証可能な MPC に基づいて実現できます。逆に、その証明を従来型の設定で生成された証明と意図的に区別できないようにすることもできます。この ZKPoK 提出のカテゴリでは、どちらの選択肢（秘密分散の設定の存在を開示する場合と秘匿する場合）も受け入れます。

contents.html: In interactive protocols, soundness is often characterized as statistical. A transformation to a non-interactive protocol can convert the statistical soundness into computational soundness (i.e., \(\kappa \leftarrow \sigma\)), which would then be too low if \(\sigma < 128\). However, it is sometimes possible to consider a tradeoff with the computational cost of the transformation.
contents.html_ja: 対話型プロトコルでは、健全性は統計的なものと特徴づけられることが多くあります。非対話型プロトコルへの変換により、統計的健全性を計算量的健全性（すなわち \(\kappa \leftarrow \sigma\)）に変換できますが、\(\sigma < 128\) の場合は低すぎることになります。ただし、変換の計算コストとのトレードオフを考慮できる場合もあります。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p104（scale 2.3）と一致。数式を LaTeX に

contents.html: For example, consider a proof generation that requires \(2^{24}\) hashings before the last random value selection that affects the input of a Fiat-Shamir transformation. By intentionally making a Fiat-Shamir transformation based on a \(2^{16}\)-iterated hashing, the computational soundness is increased by 16 bits of security while only increasing the computational complexity by less than 0.5 %. Examples of NIST-standardized iterative uses of PRFs can be found in key-derivation functions [SP800-108-Rev1], and password-based key derivation [SP800-132].
contents.html_ja: たとえば、Fiat-Shamir 変換の入力に影響する最後のランダム値の選択の前に、\(2^{24}\) 回のハッシュを必要とする証明生成を考えます。\(2^{16}\) 回反復するハッシュに基づく Fiat-Shamir 変換を意図的に行うことで、計算量的健全性は 16 ビット分のセキュリティが向上し、計算量の増加は 0.5 % 未満にとどまります。NIST が標準化した PRF の反復的な使用の例は、鍵導出関数 [SP800-108-Rev1] とパスワードベースの鍵導出 [SP800-132] に見られます。

contents.html: Some ZKPoKs (e.g., of a discrete log, of an RSA private key) may be based on specialized techniques that are somewhat similar to the operations (e.g., exponentiations) used to commit the secret. Conversely, other ZKPoKs (e.g., when proving knowledge of a pre-image of AES enciphering or of a SHA-based hashing) may stem more easily from a generic ZKP system that “arithmetizes” the statement of knowledge, the instance, and the witness in some suitable representation (e.g., specifying a Boolean or arithmetic circuit, or some other constraint system, and instantiating its input variables).

contents.html: The specification of each submitted threshold scheme will describe (in CS\(X\).3; see Section 6.3) one system model (and may identify possible variants), including the set of participants, the communication model, and the adversarial model (including goals and capabilities). The description should strive for clarity about variable options across possible deployment scenarios (e.g., DKG versus secret sharing by a dealer).

contents.html: The parties in a threshold entity. There is a “threshold entity” composed on \(n\) “parties”, collectively responsible for executing a cryptographic primitive. At the onset, all parties “know who” the \(n\) parties are and agree on \(n\) identifiers (e.g., public keys to support authenticated channels). The suitability of public keys may need to be verified (e.g., via zero-knowledge proofs) during or after the KeyGen phase.
contents.html_ja: しきい値エンティティ内の当事者。 暗号プリミティブの実行を共同で担う \(n\) 個の「当事者」から成る「しきい値エンティティ」があります。開始時に、すべての当事者は \(n\) 個の当事者が誰であるかを「知って」おり、\(n\) 個の識別子（認証されたチャネルを支える公開鍵など）に合意しています。公開鍵の適切性は、KeyGen フェーズ中またはその後に（ゼロ知識証明などで）検証する必要がある場合があります。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p105（scale 2.3）と一致。変数を LaTeX に（ソフトハイフンの語は連結）

contents.html: The assumption of an initial agreement on \(n\) identifiers is a possibility, not a requirement. A threshold scheme may be bootstrapped without prior agreement about who the \(n\) parties/identifiers are (or even the value of \(n\)), in which case the protocol may have an additional initial phase for setting up some agreement. However, that may be a distributed-systems problem outside of the scope of exploring the essential cryptographic thresholdization of the primitive at stake. A submission that considers an additional preparatory phase for the agreement of \(n\) and who the \(n\) parties are should present that phase modularly separated from the remaining threshold scheme.
contents.html_ja: \(n\) 個の識別子に関する最初の合意の仮定は、一つの可能性であって、要件ではありません。しきい値方式は、\(n\) 個の当事者・識別子が誰であるか（あるいは \(n\) の値すら）についての事前の合意なしにブートストラップされる場合もあり、その場合、プロトコルには何らかの合意を設定する追加の初期フェーズが含まれる場合があります。ただし、それは、対象となるプリミティブの本質的な暗号的しきい値化の探究の範囲外にある分散システムの問題である場合があります。\(n\) と \(n\) 個の当事者が誰であるかについての合意のための追加の準備フェーズを考慮する提出では、そのフェーズを、残りのしきい値方式からモジュール的に分離して示すべきです。

contents.html: Beneficiaries. For some operations (e.g., threshold KeyGen), the beneficiaries of the computation are the parties that end with a new secret-sharing state (possibly requiring agreement in the sense of “security with unanimous abort”), and/or an administrator (e.g., who receives a new public key). For other operations (e.g., threshold signing), the beneficiary can be an external client who requested the computation (from a threshold entity), in order to obtain an output.
contents.html_ja: 受益者。 一部の操作（しきい値 KeyGen など）では、計算の受益者は、新しい秘密分散の状態で終了する当事者（「全員一致の中断を伴う安全性」の意味での合意が必要となる場合もある）、または/および管理者（たとえば新しい公開鍵を受け取る者）です。他の操作（しきい値署名など）では、受益者は、出力を得るために（しきい値エンティティに）計算を要求した外部のクライアントである場合があります。

contents.html: Client interface. The client may or may not be aware of or be able to interact distinctively based on the \(n\)-party composition. For example, a secret sharing of the I/O can affect whether a client can separately send or receive input/output shares to or from each party.

contents.html: When the interface and rules for composition are clear, the specification of a threshold scheme should decouple the description of (i) the building blocks (e.g., consensus, reliable broadcast) of classical distributed-systems, from that of (ii) the cryptographic operations needed to support the secure multiparty computation over (or of) a secret-shared key. See Pre5 and CS\(X\).4 for recommendations about the modular specification of building blocks. The needed networking tools (e.g., broadcast) can be instantiated based on weaker resources (e.g., point-to-point channels) that are specified by referencing specifications that are free and publicly available. However, the reference implementation still needs to include code for them (see Imp2).
contents.html_ja: インタフェースと合成の規則が明確な場合、しきい値方式の仕様では、(i) 古典的な分散システムの構成要素（合意、信頼できるブロードキャストなど）の記述と、(ii) 秘密分散された鍵に対する（または鍵による）セキュアマルチパーティ計算を支えるのに必要な暗号演算の記述を、切り離すべきです。構成要素のモジュール的な仕様に関する推奨事項は、Pre5 と CS\(X\).4 を参照してください。必要なネットワークツール（ブロードキャストなど）は、無償で公開されている仕様を参照して規定される、より弱い資源（ポイントツーポイントのチャネルなど）に基づいてインスタンス化できます。ただし、参照実装には、それらのコードを含める必要があります（Imp2 を参照）。

contents.html: A baseline description may make strong assumptions about the communication network, including synchrony and transmission reliability. However, different communication environments can have different optimal threshold schemes, depending on guarantees (or the lack thereof) of synchrony, broadcast, and reliability (of message delivery). A submission should discuss the pitfalls of deploying a threshold scheme in an environment with weaker guarantees (e.g., with asynchronous and unreliable channels), and possible mitigations (see CS\(X\).5). Ideally, the security analysis (see CS\(X\).5) explains which security guarantees break across these environments.
contents.html_ja: 基準となる記述では、同期性や伝送の信頼性を含め、通信ネットワークについて強い仮定を置いてもかまいません。ただし、通信環境が異なれば、同期性、ブロードキャスト、（メッセージ配送の）信頼性の保証（またはその欠如）に応じて、最適なしきい値方式も異なりえます。提出では、より弱い保証の環境（非同期で信頼できないチャネルなど）にしきい値方式を展開する際の落とし穴と、考えられる緩和策を論じるべきです（CS\(X\).5 を参照）。理想的には、セキュリティ分析（CS\(X\).5 を参照）が、これらの環境にわたってどのセキュリティ保証が破れるかを説明します。

contents.html: In modern cryptography, security proofs are fundamental for a proper security assessment of multi-party threshold schemes. A “security proof” proves that a proposed threshold scheme satisfies a proposed security formulation in a suitable adversarial context (see Section 9.2.1). Such proof may be given by showing “emulation” of the ideal functionality, or that a non-negligible adversarial advantage in each security game implies breaking an assumption. The security analysis, which may be based on assumptions that are different from those inherent to the underlying cryptographic primitive (being thresholdized), should assess security under various compositions, including concurrent executions.

contents.html: Adaptive security (i.e., security against adaptive corruptions) may pose significant challenges in formal proofs of security, depending on the security formulation. For example, while deniability of execution may in some cases be required for indistinguishability between ideal and real executions, the use of non-committing encryption to achieve it could be excessive without a necessary practical benefit. However, a proposed protocol must not allow its critical safety properties to be trivially broken in case of adaptive corruptions, as in the classical example of a protocol that delegates all capabilities to a small quorum that is difficult to guess in advance, but which is announced during the protocol and whose overall corruption would be disastrous.
contents.html_ja: 適応的セキュリティ（すなわち、適応的な侵害に対する安全性）は、セキュリティの定式化によっては、形式的なセキュリティ証明で大きな課題となる場合があります。たとえば、理想的な実行と現実の実行の識別不可能性を保つために実行の否認可能性が必要となる場合がありますが、それを実現するための非コミット暗号の使用は、必要な実用上の利点がないまま過剰なものとなる可能性があります。ただし、提案するプロトコルは、適応的な侵害があった場合に重要な安全性の特性が自明に破られることを許してはなりません。古典的な例として、すべての能力を、事前には推測しにくい小さな定足数に委譲するものの、その定足数がプロトコル中に公表され、その全体が侵害されると壊滅的な結果になるプロトコルがあります。

contents.html: Other threshold profiles. Other threshold profiles can be considered in concrete submissions. For example, some threshold schemes may have advantageous properties when considering an even stricter honest majority, such as more than 3/4 of honest parties. For other threshold schemes, the magnitude of the number of possible quorums may matter more. For example, if a quorum is valid if and only if it has \(f + 1\) parties out of \(n\), then the number of such quorums is “\(n\) choose \(f + 1\)” (i.e., \(\binom{n}{f+1} = n!/((f+1)!(n-(f+1))!)\). A protocol may have a complexity proportional to this number \(\binom{n}{f+1}\), in which case it will stop being practical for certain parameters.
contents.html_ja: その他のしきい値プロファイル。 具体的な提出では、他のしきい値プロファイルを考慮できます。たとえば、一部のしきい値方式は、誠実な当事者が 3/4 を超えるような、さらに厳格な誠実な多数派を考えると有利な性質を持つ場合があります。他のしきい値方式では、可能な定足数の数の大きさがより重要となる場合があります。たとえば、定足数が有効であるのが \(n\) 個中 \(f + 1\) 個の当事者を含む場合に限られるなら、そのような定足数の数は「\(n\) choose \(f + 1\)」（すなわち \(\binom{n}{f+1} = n!/((f+1)!(n-(f+1))!)\)）です。プロトコルの計算量がこの数 \(\binom{n}{f+1}\) に比例する場合があり、その場合は特定のパラメータで実用的でなくなります。

contents.html: Alternative monotonic access structures. The use of the traditional term “threshold” in this Threshold Call is not meant to suppress possible submissions of schemes that are suitable for other useful and properly justified access structures. A submission may consider secret-sharing schemes and/or threshold schemes with well-specified monotonic access structures (i.e., where any superset of a quorum is also a quorum), including those that are different from a simple threshold.
contents.html_ja: 代替の単調アクセス構造。このしきい値公募で従来の「しきい値」という用語を用いるのは、他の有用で適切に正当化されたアクセス構造に適した方式の提出を抑えることを意図したものではありません。提出では、単純なしきい値とは異なるものを含め、明確に規定された単調アクセス構造（すなわち、定足数の任意の上位集合も定足数となるもの）を持つ秘密分散方式および／またはしきい値方式を検討してもよいです。

contents.html: Per §2.3 of NIST-IR8214A, there are various I/O interfaces of interest with regard to secret-sharing. The default case of secret-sharing the secret or private key is often left implicit. However, other input or output arguments can also be characterized. The baseline characterizations of interface (with regard to an identified input or output) are: not-secret-shared (NSS), secret-shared input (SSI), and secret-shared output (SSO). This section describes various cases of interest.
contents.html_ja: NIST-IR8214A の §2.3 のとおり、秘密分散に関して関心のあるさまざまな I/O インタフェースがあります。共通鍵または秘密鍵を秘密分散する既定の場合は、暗黙のままにされることが多くあります。ただし、他の入力または出力の引数も特徴付けることができます。（特定された入力または出力に関する）インタフェースの基本的な特徴付けは、秘密分散されていない（NSS）、秘密分散された入力（SSI）、秘密分散された出力（SSO）です。本節では、関心のあるさまざまなケースを説明します。

contents.html_ja: 暗黙の I/O 秘密分散モード: 鍵付きプリミティブでは、秘密鍵または共通鍵の秘密分散が既定で仮定され、これはしばしば暗黙のままにされます。

contents.html: [SSO] KeyGen. By default, a threshold KeyGen scheme produces a secret-shared output (i.e., a secret-shared secret/private key) and (when applicable) a corresponding non-secret-shared public-key counterpart.
contents.html_ja: [SSO] KeyGen。既定では、しきい値 KeyGen 方式は、秘密分散された出力（すなわち、秘密分散された共通鍵または秘密鍵）と、（該当する場合）対応する秘密分散されていない公開鍵の対を生成します。

contents.html: Subsequent [SSI] operation. After the KeyGen (produced by a dealer or via a DKG), the subsequent threshold operation (e.g., signing) uses the private/secret key as a secret-shared input to retain its confidentiality.
contents.html_ja: 後続の [SSI] 操作。KeyGen（ディーラーまたは DKG によって生成されたもの）の後、後続のしきい値操作（署名など）では、機密性を保つため、秘密鍵または共通鍵を秘密分散された入力として使用します。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p110（scale 1.4）の画像と照合し一致

contents.html: Since the secret sharings in these modes are assumed by default, the modes can be referred to as non-secret-sharing (NSS) modes when no other input or output (i.e., besides the private key) are secret-shared.
contents.html_ja: これらのモードでは秘密分散が既定で仮定されるため、他の入力または出力（すなわち秘密鍵以外）が秘密分散されない場合、これらのモードを秘密分散なし（NSS）モードと呼ぶことができます。

contents.html: SSO-decryption. A threshold decryption can be in SSO mode with regard to the decrypted plaintext. This can be useful for pair-wise key-agreement (2KA) when one side (thresholdized) decapsulates the key-contribution sent by the other side.
contents.html_ja: SSO 復号。 しきい値復号は、復号された平文に関して SSO モードにできます。これは、一方の側（しきい値化されたもの）が、他方の側から送られた鍵の寄与をデカプセル化する、2 者間の鍵合意（2KA）に有用です。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p110（scale 1.4）の画像と照合し一致

contents.html: SSI-encryption. A threshold public-key encryption can be in SSI mode with regard to the plaintext, which may be a secret for use in another context.
contents.html_ja: SSI 暗号化。 しきい値公開鍵暗号化は、平文に関して SSI モードにできます。平文は、別の文脈で使う秘密である場合があります。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p111（scale 1.4）の画像と照合し一致

contents.html: SSO-KA. In an ECC-2KA (a la Diffie-Hellman), the EC-primitive (e.g., CDH or MQV; see Appendix A.4.1.2) produces an output that will seed an agreed key. If one party is thresholdized, their output should be in SSO mode.
contents.html_ja: SSO-KA。 ECC-2KA（Diffie-Hellman 方式）では、EC プリミティブ（CDH や MQV など。附属書 A.4.1.2 を参照）が、合意される鍵のシードとなる出力を生成します。一方の当事者がしきい値化される場合、その出力は SSO モードであるべきです。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p111（scale 1.4）の画像と照合し一致

contents.html: SSI signing. A threshold signing can keep the message private by using an SSI mode with regard to the message. However, the needed threshold hashing then brings a significant overhead. If, instead, the message hash is secret-shared by a dealer (e.g., a client who is requesting the signature computation), then each party in the threshold scheme directly receives a secret share of the message hash (or, as applicable, of the hash of a combination of various public elements and the message).
contents.html_ja: SSI 署名。しきい値署名は、メッセージに関して SSI モードを使うことで、メッセージの機密性を保てます。ただし、そのために必要なしきい値ハッシュには、大きなオーバーヘッドが伴います。代わりに、メッセージのハッシュがディーラー（署名計算を要求するクライアントなど）によって秘密分散される場合、しきい値方式の各当事者は、メッセージのハッシュ（または、該当する場合、さまざまな公開要素とメッセージの組み合わせのハッシュ）の秘密シェアを直接受け取ります。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p111（scale 1.4）の画像と照合し一致
contents.translation_resolve_note: secret share は同資料で「秘密シェア」

contents.html: SSIO signing. An SSIO mode (combining SSI and SSO) can be useful in privacy-enhancing contexts (e.g., for a time-stamping service). For example, a client can provide shares of a message hash to a threshold entity, and then receive signature shares. The result is similar to a blind-signing service, except that (i) the signing key is further thresholdized, and (ii) the knowledge of the message/signature is within the theoretical reach of a threshold coalition of signer-parties.
contents.html_ja: SSIO 署名。SSIO モード（SSI と SSO の組み合わせ）は、プライバシー強化の文脈（タイムスタンプサービスなど）で有用となりえます。たとえば、クライアントがメッセージハッシュのシェアをしきい値エンティティに提供し、その後署名シェアを受け取ることができます。結果はブラインド署名サービスに似ていますが、(i) 署名用秘密鍵がさらにしきい値化されている点と、(ii) メッセージ・署名に関する知識が、署名者のしきい値連合の理論上の到達範囲内にある点が異なります。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p111（scale 1.4）の画像と照合し一致

contents.html: Provided that at least the default private/secret key is secret-shared, a submission can choose to cover one or more secret-sharing interfaces (i.e., NSS, SSI, SSO, SSIO) for any of the other input or output elements. Some correctness challenges with SSI and SSO modes may be resolved with ZKPs or/and verifiable secret-sharing modes.
contents.html_ja: 少なくとも既定の秘密鍵または共通鍵が秘密分散されていれば、提出では、他の入力要素または出力要素のいずれについても、1 つ以上の秘密分散インタフェース（すなわち NSS、SSI、SSO、SSIO）を対象とすることを選べます。SSI と SSO のモードに伴う正しさの課題の一部は、ZKP または検証可能な秘密分散モード、あるいはその両方で解決できる場合があります。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p111（scale 1.4）の画像と照合し一致
contents.translation_resolve_note: private/secret key は秘密鍵または共通鍵

contents.html: A proposal of threshold scheme that receives an SSI input (including a secret-shared key) may be based on an explicit assumption that the secret-shared input is correct. For example, this is the case if the input is obtained from a previous secure threshold execution (e.g., a DKG), or from a trustworthy dealer, or has been verified as correct after having been dealt by an untrusted dealer. Alternatively, the threshold scheme may be devised to be inherently resilient against a malicious secret sharing, (e.g., by starting with a joint computation to confirm correctness of the secret-shared state).
contents.html_ja: SSI 入力（秘密分散された鍵を含む）を受け取るしきい値方式の提案は、秘密分散された入力が正しいという明示的な仮定に基づいてもかまいません。たとえば、入力が、以前の安全なしきい値実行（DKG など）から得られた場合、信頼できるディーラーから得られた場合、または信頼できないディーラーによって配布された後に正しいと検証された場合が、これに当たります。あるいは、しきい値方式を、悪意のある秘密分散に対して本質的に耐性を持つように考案してもかまいません（たとえば、秘密分散された状態の正しさを確認する共同計算から始めることで）。

Preface

For transparency and involvement, the Threshold Call was widely disseminated in advance, inviting public comments on an initial public draft (ipd) [NIST-IR8214C-ipd; PubComsIPD] and a second public draft (2pd) [NIST-IR8214C-2pd; PubComs2PD]. It was presented at inter national cryptography events, and promoted in various NIST workshops, such as the NIST Workshop on Multi-Party Threshold Schemes (MPTS) 2023, the Special Topics on Privacy and Public Auditability 6th event (STPPA6), and the NIST Workshop on Privacy-Enhancing Cryptography (WPEC) 2024. Also, (MPTS) 2026 is near simultaneous with this publication.

Toy parametrization. If the conditions of Requirement 8.2 are in place, then a toy parametrization can, for example, aim for 𝜅 ≈ 16 bits of “security strength” and then extrapolate what are the expected performance results for a secure parametrization with 𝜅 ≈ 128. For example, suppose that the memory complexity is quadratic (𝒪(𝜅2)), in the security parameter 𝜅. If, simultaneously, the needed memory for evaluating a threshold scheme is linear in the number of parties, then the toy parametrization allows (for this metric) evaluating 64 times more parties than the configuration with realistic parameters (𝜅 ≈ 128).

Toy Configuration for Didactic Purposes. Even when the Baseline Platform can execute and test with realistic parameters, the specification and evaluation of a toy parametrization is also welcome for didactic or verification purposes. For example, such toy configuration could be akin to testing RSA encryption and decryption when the modulus is 𝑁 = 43× 67, instead of having at ≥ 3,072 bits. This may ease the understanding, or even enable a more extensive coverage of KAT vector testing (e.g., if otherwise the vectors would be too large).
The configurations can be indexed (e.g., Cfg , Cfg , ...) in order to allow easy

referencing in the subsequent sections with measurements and analysis. Also, the indexations can be parametric, e.g., using Cfg (𝑛, 𝑓) where 𝑛 is the total number 1 of parties and 𝑓 is the number of parties corrupted in some specified manner.

The symbol ≳ denotes “greater than or approximately equal to”, in order to allow a small slack. For example, it can be acceptable to consider a protocol that uses standard “128-bit” parameters (e.g., AES-128) but then the security estimate only guarantees at least 125 bits of security. This slack is also assumed implicit in the PQ categories when using the symbol ≥ (“greater than or equal to”), since there the parameter 𝜃 is discrete. The strength is also dependent on the computational complexity (e.g., a Boolean gate or a full-fledged AES evaluation) equated to one bit of strength, which is often left implicit.

Threshold KeyGen (DKG). Threshold KeyGen schemes are usually known as distributed key generation (DKG) protocols. They enable a set of parties to collaborate to generate a secret sharing of a fresh secret or private key, such that the key is never assembled in one place. When applicable, the parties also obtain the public key (e.g., an RSA modulus, usually not secret-shared, obtained from the product of two secret primes),
and/or commitments of everyone’s private keys. Some domain parameters are agreed upon before the DKG (e.g., elliptic curve, security strength 𝜅, RSA public encryption key 𝑒).

The goal of a DKG for an ECC scheme is to produce a secret-sharing [𝑑] of the private key 𝑑, produce commitments of the shares 𝑑 of each party, and calculate the public key 𝑖 𝑄 = 𝑑 ⋅ 𝐺. The “commitments” may be simple public-key shares 𝑄 = 𝑑 ⋅ 𝐺, or fancier
𝑖 𝑖
semantically hiding commitments. The KeyGen may include additional elements related to the commitments (e.g., a ZKPoK of each secret share).

The optimization of threshold schemes may suggest different encodings or representations that are mathematically equiv alent (e.g., whether/when to use the Number Theoretic Transform (NTT) and its inverse NTT−1). This may be done, provided that the keys are interchangeable with regard to a subsequent threshold operation (i.e., signing, decryption or encryption).
For any of the two ML-based schemes, the parties may use a secure coin-flipping protocol to collaboratively determine the public seed 𝜌, and then use it in the clear to pseudoran
𝐀̂
. The parties may then interact in a threshold manner

domly generate the public matrix to distributively generate a secret sharing (across the parties) of the needed vector terms: (𝐬,̂ 𝐞)̂ for K-PKE, and (𝐬 ,𝐬 ) for ML-DSA. Finally, the parties may distributively compute

the result of the linear operation between the matrix and the vectors: 𝐭̂ = 𝐀̂ ∘ 𝐬̂ + 𝐞,̂ for K-PKE; or 𝐭 = NTT−1(𝐀̂ ∘ NTT(𝐬 )) + 𝐬 , for ML-DSA. In the case of ML-DSA, the 𝟏 𝟐 element 𝐾 would also be distributively produced as a secret sharing. The private and public keys are then the applicable encodings of the computed elements.

11.5.2. Conventional FHE

Category S5 relates to fully-homomorphic encryption (FHE), which is a special type of encryption scheme that allows for arbitrary computation over encrypted data. Besides the usual operations of KeyGen, encryption (Enc), and decryption (Dec), it also allows for homomorphic evaluation (hom). Given one or more ciphertexts, produced via Enc, the hom operation can be used to produce a new ciphertext that encrypts the result of an intended operation over the original plaintexts. This operation is performed without the original plaintext and the decryption key. Appendix B.1 has additional details.
The Technical Specification shall explain at least the interface and properties of the four main algorithms: KeyGen, Enc, Dec, hom.

The specification of homomorphic evaluation (hom) can include a set of related algorithms, covering various homomorphic operations. Depending on the FHE scheme, it may be useful to modularize the specification of other auxiliary algorithms, such as for refreshing a ciphertext (i.e., a bootstrapping to reduce the internal noise).

ZKPoK security strength. Per Section 9.1, the submission of a ZKPoK will indicate a parameter set for achieving at least one profile of security strength for soundness and zero-knowledge, satisfying (𝜅, 𝜎) ≳ (128, 40). The proposal of a second parameter set achieving (𝜅, 𝜎) ≳ (192, 64) is also encouraged. See also Appendix B.2.4.

Conventional signature. ML-DSA [FIPS-204] is one of the two first NIST-standardized stateless PQ signing schemes. Its construction is inspired by Schnorr signatures, but it is based on lattices in order to achieve quantum resistance, and includes various tweaks for efficiency and security. The standard defines three parametrizations: ML-DSA{44,65,87}, equating them to PQC security categories (𝜃) {2, 3, 5}, respectively. Correspondingly, the internal generations of random bits are required to use security strength 𝜅 at least {128, 192, 256}. However, if ML-DSA-44 is implemented with randomness with strength 128 ≤ 𝜅 < 192, then its claimed PQC security category is decreased to 𝜃 = 1 [FIPS-204, §3.6.1].

Pure, pre-hashed, and internal function. ML-DSA has two main versions: “pure” (ML-DSA) and “pre-hashed” (HashML-DSA). Both versions accept an input argument with context (i.e., a byte string 𝑐𝑡𝑥 with length between 0 and 255). The pre-hashed version also receives as input an identifier of which hash function to use. The specification modularizes an internal algorithm ML-DSA.Sign_internal(𝑠𝑘, 𝑀′, 𝑟𝑛𝑑), where the input 𝑀′ already integrates the context and the plaintext message or its hash.

A standalone ML-DSA signature does not reveal which mode was used. In particular, the deterministic mode is not verifiably deterministic. Per FIPS 204 (Algorithm 7, step 7), the internal signing algorithm ML-DSA.Sign_internal(𝑠𝑘, 𝑀′, 𝑟𝑛𝑑) obtains a secret random or pseudorandom) value 𝜌″ ← 𝐻(𝐾||𝑟𝑛𝑑||𝜇, 64), where 𝐾 is derived from the private key, 𝑟𝑛𝑑 is all zeros or random, and 𝜇 is derived from the message and the public key.

One peculiarity of ML-DSA signing is that it requires a rejection sampling loop. Without it, there would be a noticeable probability that a signature would reveal information about the secret key. Therefore, the rejection sampling keeps trying until it obtains a signature candidate that satisfies a number of tests. In FIPS-204, Table 1 lists the expected number of trials: {4.25, 5.1, 3.85} for ML-DSA-{44,65,87}, respectively. The publication also lists iteration bounds for a non-completion probability around 2−256.

The Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (SLH-DSA) is a post-quantum signature scheme standardized by FIPS-205. Its security does not rely on keeping track of which internal signing keys have been used. As components, SLH-DSA uses two other hash-based signature schemes: the forest of random subsets (FORS), and the eXtended Merkle Signature Scheme (XMSS). In turn, XMSS is based on the Winternitz One-Time Signature Plus (WOTS+) scheme. The XMSS scheme is used within a hypertree signature scheme, which uses a tree of trees, rather than a single XMSS tree.

SLH-DSA specifies 12 parameter sets that correspond to 2 × 3 × 2 options (see Table 12 of FIPS-205): SLH-DSA-{SHA2,SHAKE}-{128,192,256}{s,f}, More sets (e.g., allowing fewer but shorter signatures) may be allowed by the forthcoming SP800-230. The intermediate label {128,192,256} indicates a corresponding claimed PQC security category 𝜃 = {1, 3, 5}. For each such level there are four possible parameter sets, resulting from a choice of hash/XOF family {SHA2,SHAKE}, and a mode from between “s” (relatively small signa tures) and “f” (relatively fast signature generation). Furthermore, the standard defines a “pure” version (SLH-DSA) and a “pre-hash” version (HashSLH-DSA). These options enable choosing whether to provide the entire message or just its hash to the core signing algorithm.

The approved stateful HBS schemes are Leighton-Micali Signature (LMS), specified by reference to RFC8554, and XMSS, specified by reference to RFC8391. They are both based on the Winternitz signature scheme. Additionally, their “multi-tree” variants — the Hierarchical Signature System (HSS) and the multi-tree XMSS (XMSSMT), respectively — are also approved. The multi-tree version allows for a more efficient way of determining the public key. SP800-208 also specifies a modified version of XMSS and XMSSMT, to distribute (not in a secret-shared sense) the implementation across multiple cryptographic modules.

Primitives of interest. Enc outputs a ciphertext 𝐶 = Enc(𝑝𝑢𝑏𝐾𝑒𝑦, 𝑀[, 𝑅]), as an encryption of an input plaintext message 𝑀, using a public encryption key 𝑝𝑢𝑏𝐾𝑒𝑦, and op tionally (i.e., depending on the scheme) a random value 𝑅 that directly enables probabilistic encryption. Correspondingly, Dec outputs the original plaintext 𝑀 = Dec(𝑝𝑟𝑖𝑣𝐾𝑒𝑦, 𝐶), as decryption of an input ciphertext, using the private decryption key 𝑝𝑟𝑖𝑣𝐾𝑒𝑦.

In the (informally called) “textbook” RSA-PKE, the KeyGen (see category N4.2) generates a public RSA modulus 𝑁 (product of two secret primes), a public encryption key 𝑒, and a private decryption key 𝑑. In subcategory N2.1, the core encryption/decryption primitives are:

RSA Encryption Primitive (RSAEP): Obtains a ciphertext 𝑐 = RSAEP(𝑒, 𝑚) = 𝑚𝑒 mod 𝑁, using the public key 𝑒 to encrypt the plaintext 𝑚. RSAEP is assumed to be a one-way function. Being deterministic, it does not provide on its own the IND-CPA property of an encryption scheme. Providing semantic security and beyond requires a higher-level construction (see §A.2.1.2), including randomness.

RSA Decryption Primitive (RSADP): Recovers the plaintext 𝑚 = 𝑐𝑑modN, by calculating 𝑚 = RSADP(𝑝𝑟𝑖𝑣𝐾𝑒𝑦, 𝑐), where the private key privKey is used to decrypt the ciphertext 𝑐. The input privKey is acceptable in three possible formats [SP800-56B-Rev2, §6.2.2]: basic (𝑁, 𝑑), prime-factor (𝑝, 𝑞, 𝑑), and Chinese-remainder theorem (CRT) (𝑁, 𝑒, 𝑑, 𝑝, 𝑞,𝑑𝑃, 𝑑𝑄, 𝑞𝐼𝑛𝑣), where [SP800-56B-Rev2, §3.2] (𝑝, 𝑞) is the pair of secret prime factors of 𝑁, 𝑑𝑃 is 𝑑 mod (𝑝 − 1), 𝑑𝑄 is 𝑑 mod (𝑞 − 1), and 𝑞𝐼𝑛𝑣 is the inverse of 𝑞 mod 𝑝.

FIPS-203 is the first NIST standard to specify a PQ-PKE scheme (dubbed K-PKE), whose use is only approved to support ML-KEM. The present subcategory (N2.2) is interested in the core K-PKE encryption/decryption primitives: K-PKE.Encrypt (Enc) and K-PKE.Decrypt (Dec). The Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) FIPS-197 includes an encryption (Enc) algorithm Enc(𝐾, 𝑀) = 𝑃 and a decryption (Dec) algorithm Dec(𝐾, 𝐶) = 𝑃, where 𝐾 is the key (with 128, 192, or 256 bits), 𝑃 is the 128-bit plaintext, and 𝐶 is the 128-bit ciphertext.
Enc(𝐾, 𝑁, 𝐴, 𝑃 ) = (𝐶, 𝑇 )
Dec(𝐾, 𝑁, 𝐴, 𝐶, 𝑇 ) = {output 𝑃 if 𝑇 is valid, and output fail otherwise},

where 𝐾 is the 128-bit 𝑘𝑒𝑦, 𝑁 is the 128-bit nonce, 𝐴 is an optional associated data, 𝑃 is an arbitrary-length plaintext, 𝐶 is the ciphertext (with the same width as 𝑃), and 𝑇 is a 128-bit authentication tag (truncatable).

One variant mode uses a 256-bit key, from which the extra 128 bits are used to XOR-mask the input nonce, in order to retain 128 bits of security in a multi-key setting. In that case, Enc(𝐾||𝐾′, 𝑁, 𝐴, 𝑃 ) = Enc(𝐾, 𝑁 ⊕ 𝐾′, 𝐴, 𝑃 ).

Hash functions. The syntax for hashing is Hash(𝑀) = 𝐻, where 𝑀 is the plaintext (i.e., message) and 𝐻 is the output hash. The hash functions of interest for benchmarking in the threshold setting are those with non-truncated output and output length ≥ 224, from:

Extendable output functions (XOF). The basic syntax for XOF’ing is XOF(𝑀, 𝐿) = 𝐻, where 𝑀 is the plaintext (i.e., message), 𝐿 is the XOF output length, and 𝐻 is the output. A XOF with a pre-defined length is essentially a hash function. Some XOFs are “customizable” via additional input parameters. The XOFs of interest are those based on Keccak and Ascon:
• SHAKE128, SHAKE256 [FIPS-202]

Customizable XOFs. cSHAKE128 and cSHAKE256 are customizable with a “function name” parameter 𝑁 (e.g., “KMAC” when used as part of the “KMAC” algorithm) and a customization bit-string 𝑆. If 𝑁 and 𝑆 are empty, then cSHAKE matches the original SHAKE. Ascon-CXOF128 accepts an extra parameter “Z” (customization bit string). However, using 𝑍 as an empty string in Ascon-CXOF128 yields a different function (i.e., not Ascon-XOF128).

The high-level syntax for MAC’ing is 𝑇 = MAC(𝐾, 𝑀), where 𝐾 is the key, 𝑀 is a message of arbitrary length, and 𝑇 is the output tag. Depending on the MAC scheme, there may be constraints on the lengths of the input key and output tag. Some MAC constructions allow additional parameters to specify the output length and even a cus tomizable string to adjust the function (akin to domain separation). Depending on the application, a tag truncation (to 𝜆 bits) can also be considered, but is hereafter ignored.
CMAC [SP800-38B] and GMAC [SP800-38D], based on AES. In terms of key length, CMAC-AES-* and GMAC-AES-* use a *-bit key, where ∗ ∈ {128, 256}.

KMAC [SP800-185], based on cSHAKE. KMAC*(𝐾, 𝑋, 𝐿, 𝑆) uses cSHAKE*, where ∗ ∈ {128, 256}, 𝐾 is the key (of arbitrary length, possibly 0), 𝑋 is the plaintext, 𝐿 is the output tag length, and 𝑆 is an optional customization string (possibly empty). A related construction KMACXOF*, with input/output syntax similar to its counterpart KMAC*, allows for specifying 𝐿 after the algorithm starts computing.
Sample a random positive integer 𝑑 (mod 𝑛, the order of the subgroup of interest).
Perform a scalar multiplication to obtain the corresponding public key 𝑄 = 𝑑 ⋅ 𝐺.

“Scalar multiplication” versus “exponentiation”. Group operations over elliptic curves are usually described with additive notation. When a public key 𝑄 is determined by a repeated sum of the base-point 𝐺, a secret number 𝑑 of times, their relationship is mathematically expressed as a scalar multiplication (i.e., 𝑄 = 𝑑 ⋅ 𝐺). However, the literature often refers to this as an “exponentiation”, and correspondingly identifies the secret key as the “discrete log” of the public key. This a tolerated misnomer due to the prior popularization of schemes described with multiplicative notation (e.g., 𝑞 = 𝑔𝑑).

EdDSA. The scheme uses a precursor private key 𝑑 to pseudorandomly derive a private signing key 𝑠 and a nonce-derivation key 𝜈, as (𝑠, 𝜈) = Hash(𝑑). The private signing key is then used to derive the public key 𝑄 = 𝑠⋅𝐺. The generation of 𝜈 is op tional in the threshold setting, since interchangeable signatures (with regard to verifi cation) can be produced without using the nonce-derivation key (see Appendix A.1.1).
ECDSA. The scheme requires establishing a private signing key (𝑑 in ECDSA), and a corresponding public key 𝑄 = 𝑑 ⋅ 𝐺. The private key is later used to produce signatures (see Appendix A.1.2).

2KA. In a threshold 2KA scheme, each party may need a secret sharing of a static private key 𝑑 (or 𝑑 ) and/or an ephemeral private key (𝑑 ). After the private 𝐴 𝑠,𝐴 𝑒,𝐴 keys are generated, the side holding them in a secret-shared manner needs to use them (in a subsequent CDH or MQV operation of the 2KA protocol) as the scalar by which to multiply the public key of the other party, and let the result still be in SSO mode (see Appendix A.4.1.2).

The size of an RSA modulus determines an upper bound on the security strength of the RSA-related primitive (i.e., signing, encryption or decryption). The following specific cases are fixed: |𝑁| = 3072 for 𝜅 ≈ 128, |𝑁| = 7680 for 𝜅 ≈ 192, and |𝑁| = 15360 for 𝜅 ≈ 256. By standard, the RSA modulus length |𝑁| must be a multiple of 8. For benchmarking pur poses, this Threshold Call further suggests that it be a multiple of 512. Implementations that aim for 𝜅 ∉ {128, 192, 256} can interpolate an RSA modulus size by rounding up to a multi ple of 512 the solution (for |𝑁|) of 𝜅 ln(2) = √3 (64/9) ⋅ (|𝑁| ln(2)) ⋅ ln2(|𝑁| ln(2))−4.69, from “§7.5 Strength of Key Establishment Methods” of the “FIPS 140-2 Implementation Guidance” [IG-FIPS-140-2]. Conventional generation. Various primitives require a randomly generated secret bit-string or secret integer within an interval, without the need for a corresponding public com ponent. For example, this is the case for an AES key, a secret-key for encapsulation under an RSA PKE, a nonce for use in other schemes, and a salt for a KDM or KC in the scope of a 2KA. Usually, these KeyGens are required to follow NIST-approved RBG methods [SP800-90A-R1; SP800-90B; SP800-90C], to obtain either pseudorandomness or true randomness.

B.1 Category S5: Fully-Homomorphic Encryption (FHE)

Category S5 (see submission requirements in Section 11.5) allows for the submission of FHE schemes. Informally speaking, an FHE scheme allows for arbitrary computations over encrypted data. Being an encryption scheme, in includes KeyGen, encryption (Enc) and decryption (Dec) algorithms Being fully homomorphic it also includes algorithms for the efficient homomorphic evaluation, over the ciphertext space (𝒞), of a “complete basis” of operations from the plaintext space (𝒫) (e.g., see Ref. [HES, §1.1.1]). The composition of these operations allows for arbitrary computations.

Traditionally, the complete basis over 𝒫 is composed of addition and multiplication, such as {xor, and} over GF(2), or {+, ×} over a field modulo a large prime. More precisely (though for simplicity leaving the key implicit), suppose that a function 𝑓 ∶ 𝒫 → 𝒫 or a binary operation 𝑜𝑝 ∶ 𝒫 × 𝒫 → 𝒫 over the plaintext space can be specified as a composition of operations in the supported basis. In an “oblivious” PRF evaluation there is a client (𝐴) holding a secret plaintext 𝑚, and a server (𝑆) holding a secret key 𝑘. They interact in a way that allows the client to privately learn the output of the PRF evaluation over the plaintext, while both parties remain oblivious to the other party’s input. By replacing the PRF with the AES blockcipher (a PRP), the client learns the AES-enciphering of the plaintext 𝑚. Oblivious AES-enciphering is a typical benchmark case for secure 2-party computation, typically using techniques such as garbled circuits and/or oblivious transfer. Compared with an FHE-based solution, usual S2PC protocols lead to faster execution, but also larger communication complexity.

In usual ZKP terminology [ZkpComRef], a ZKPoK is used to prove a statement of knowl edge, such as knowledge of a secret witness (𝑤) that satisfies a given relation (𝑅) with a public instance (𝑥) such that 𝑅(𝑥, 𝑤) is true. For example, a ZKPoK of a private RSA key can have as instance the public RSA modulus 𝑁, as secret witness the pair (𝑝, 𝑞) of prime factors, and as relation the predicate that returns true if and only if the input instance 𝑁 is a valid product of two secret primes. Additional refinements can be considered (e.g., proving the two primes have the same bit-length, and are both 3 mod 4).

In interactive protocols, soundness is often characterized as statistical. A transformation to a non-interactive protocol can convert the statistical soundness into computational soundness (i.e., 𝜅 ← 𝜎), which would then be too low if 𝜎 < 128. However, it is sometimes possible to consider a tradeoff with the computational cost of the transformation.

For example, consider a proof generation that requires 224 hashings before the last random value selection that affects the input of a Fiat-Shamir transformation. By intentionally mak ing a Fiat-Shamir transformation based on a 216-iterated hashing, the computational sound ness is increased by 16 bits of security while only increasing the computational complexity by less than 0.5 %. Examples of NIST-standardized iterative uses of PRFs can be found in key-derivation functions [SP800-108-Rev1], and password-based key derivation [SP800-132].

The specification of each submitted threshold scheme will describe (in CS𝑋.3; see Sec tion 6.3) one system model (and may identify possible variants), including the set of partic ipants, the communication model, and the adversarial model (including goals and capabil ities). In addition to the actual “parties” that hold the secret-shared keys, the system may include coordinators, administrators, clients and other devices (e.g., routers, clocks, RBGs). The model needs to explain how the parties are activated (e.g., via an authorized/authenti cated client request, or by an administrator) and describe the applicable input/output secret-sharing interfaces (see Appendix C.4). The description should strive for clarity about variable options across possible deployment scenarios (e.g., DKG versus secret sharing by a dealer).

The parties in a threshold entity. There is a “threshold entity” composed on 𝑛 “parties”, collectively responsible for executing a cryptographic primitive. At the onset, all parties “know who” the 𝑛 parties are and agree on 𝑛 identifiers (e.g., public keys to support authenticated channels). The suitability of public keys may need to be verified (e.g., via zero-knowledge proofs) during or after the KeyGen phase.

The assumption of an initial agreement on 𝑛 identifiers is a possibility, not a requirement. A threshold scheme may be bootstrapped without prior agreement about who the 𝑛 parties/i dentifiers are (or even the value of 𝑛), in which case the protocol may have an additional initial phase for setting up some agreement. However, that may be a distributed-systems problem outside of the scope of exploring the essential cryptographic thresholdization of the primitive at stake. A submission that considers an additional preparatory phase for the agreement of 𝑛 and who the 𝑛 parties are should present that phase modularly separated from the remaining threshold scheme.

Client interface. The client may or may not be aware of or be able to interact distinctively based on the 𝑛-party composition. This ability can be affected by the input/output (I/O) interface (see Appendix C.4). For example, a secret sharing of the I/O can affect whether a client can separately send or receive input/output shares to or from each party.

The security analysis required in CS𝑋.5 refers to the logical specification of the threshold scheme (CS𝑋.3–CS𝑋.4). Comments about implementation or deployment security are also welcome, including in CS𝑋.7.

Motivating adoption. There is value in identifying motivating applications for the adoption of threshold schemes in each threshold profile. Therefore, the submission should identify (in CS𝑋.7) use-cases for which the proposed threshold ranges are adequate.
The following nomenclature is defined to conveniently identify some default threshold profiles, based on the total number of parties and/or some corruption threshold (𝑓) assumed clear in the context.

The default profiles exclude the cases 𝑓 = 0 and 𝑓 = 𝑛. Therefore, for the “two”-party profile (with 𝑛 = 2) — the usual secure two-party computation (S2PC) setting — only the “dishonest majority” case matters (with 𝑓 = 1). For the “three”-party profile, the 2/3 honest majority case does not apply.

For each primitive (see Sections 10 and 11) considered for thresholdization, a variety of solutions is possible across threshold parametrizations. Therefore, it is useful to consider the notion of “threshold profile”, defining a suitable threshold-parametrization range for secure operations. The threshold profile should characterize at least the total number (𝑛) of parties, and the various corruption thresholds (𝑓) and participation thresholds (𝑘). The plural is used in “thresholds” since the thresholds can vary depending on which security property is being evaluated. This is the NIST Threshold Call, calling for public submissions of multi-party threshold schemes, and other related crypto-systems, to support the United States’ National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) in gathering a public body of reference materials on advanced cryptography. In a threshold scheme, a reference cryptographic primitive (e.g., signing, encryption, decryption, key generation) is computed in a distributed manner, while its private/secret key is or becomes secret-shared across various parties. The threshold schemes submitted in reply to this call will be interchangeable with a reference non-threshold primitive of interest, in the sense that their outputs can be used interchangeably in a subsequent operation. The primitives of interest are organized into various categories, across two classes: Class N, for selected NIST-specified primitives; and Class S, for special primitives that are not specified by NIST but are threshold friendly or have useful functional features. The scope of Class S also includes fully-homomorphic encryption, zero-knowledge proofs, and auxiliary gadgets. This document specifies submission phases, and the requirements for submitting a package, including a technical specification, a reference implementation, and a report on experimental evaluation. A subsequent phase of public analysis will support the elaboration of a characterization report, which may help assess new interests beyond the cryptographic techniques currently standardized by NIST, and may include recommendations for future processes.

Crypto-systems; distributed systems; fully-homomorphic encryption (FHE); post-quantum cryptography (PQC); secure multiparty computation (MPC); threshold cryptography; threshold encryption; threshold schemes; threshold signatures; zero-knowledge proofs (ZKP)

From a standardization perspective, the exploration of “advanced” cryptography is a chal lenging endeavor. It may require “advanced” or custom processes, addressing challenging questions: Focus on building blocks or protocols? Which security properties to require? How to cover a vast range of possibilities? What and when to standardize or recommend?

This “NIST First Call for Multi-Party Threshold Schemes” (or, simply, “Threshold Call”) establishes a process for developing a high-quality body of reference materials, to be open for public analysis. The call stands at the threshold of advanced cryptography, proposing an exploration of multi-party computation (MPC) techniques, namely threshold schemes. These allow distribution of trust in the implementation of cryptographic primitives, including those standardized by NIST, and others with special useful properties. Fully-homomorphic encryption (FHE) and zero-knowledge proofs (ZKP) are also within the scope of interest.

The envisioned process relies on international community engagement by multiple teams of experts. A “Previews” phase will enable early presentation of plans of future package submissions, to foster public awareness and discussion, in time for adaptations. Each submission package can propose multiple crypto-systems, developed by collaborative teams.

This document is intended for the following audience: cryptography experts interested in providing constructive technical feedback, or collaborating in the development of open reference materials; all those, in academia, industry, government, and the general pub lic, who are interested in the development and use of threshold schemes and advanced cryptography, including corresponding best practices and recommendations.

The authors also thank Isabel Van Wyk, from NIST, for various editorial comments.
